diagnosis: The image shows a machine-precision jam: hundreds of tightest pairs have slack below about \(5\times10^{-16}\), there are no rattlers, and most points have roughly 43–46 contacts. With \(54\cdot22\) tangential coordinates, this heavily overconstrained contact graph explains why LP polishing gained only \(3.15\times10^{-7}\) and why random kicks either return to the same basin or produce worse configurations; several attempts also wasted the search by exceeding the time limit. Structurally, most points appear non-tight with only about eight partners, suggesting an approximate partition into six blocks of nine points, with inter-block pairs at the maximum and intra-block pairs below it. That clean block/association-scheme structure is blurred in the incumbent—several points have only 23–38 contacts—so further undirected continuous polishing is unlikely to discover the missing discrete topology.

diagnosis: All successful programs start from the published record and merely LP-polish it, improving the cosine by only $3.15\times10^{-7}$, while most basin-hopping variants either return to the same point or time out. The image explains why: roughly 330 pairs are tied at the maximum within about $10^{-15}$, every point has between 23 and 47 contacts, and there are no rattlers, so this is an extremely jammed, nearly degenerate optimum whose active constraints are indistinguishable at machine precision. Small perturbations are pulled back by the LP, whereas large random kicks destroy too much structure and are rejected or consume the whole budget in repeated full LPs. The configuration is also structurally irregular: contact counts vary by a factor of two, the principal-axis projection has outliers and no visible orbit structure, and there is no evidence of the balanced stress, centroid cancellation, and frame isotropy expected from a highly symmetric optimal code.

diagnosis: Our best score 0.0476076014133 is only 3.15e-07 below the published record and was achieved by the seed LP polish; essentially all 49 programs, including basin-hopping variants, return to the same optimum. The image explains why: roughly the 330 tightest pairs are tied at the maximum to within ~1e-15, there are 0 rattlers, and every point carries ~23–46 contacts, so the configuration is an over-jammed, rigid contact network in which any single-point or isotropic random kick either snaps back under LP polishing or destroys competitiveness and cannot be recovered within the time limit (several attempts simply timed out). What the best solution is missing is structural slack heterogeneity — a new basin almost certainly needs a sparser, non-uniform contact graph with some near-rattler/low-contact points and/or an organised (clustered or orbit-symmetric) topology that permits collective rearrangement, whereas the current PCA-projected contact graph is a dense, featureless hairball with no movable subset. Real progress therefore requires topology-changing moves that respect or deliberately rewire the contact graph, run under strict internal deadlines well below 180 s.

diagnosis: The best code is stuck in an extremely jammed local optimum, with at least 330 pairs tied at the maximum cosine to within $10^{-15}$ and every point carrying 23--46 contacts with zero rattlers, so the LP polish has no feasible descent direction at machine precision. Small perturbations are pulled straight back to the same active contact set by re-polishing, while large kicks produce configurations too poor to recover, and several heavier attempts simply timed out past the 180s limit before returning anything. The contact graph in the PCA projection is a dense, amorphous hairball with no clusters, symmetry, or block structure to exploit. The missing structural property is therefore a qualitatively different, sparser or more regular contact topology -- likely with a few genuinely loose points or an algebraic/orbit structure -- rather than any further tightening of the current graph.
